words.group: Spelling: double letters and silent endings
words.childMeaning: To make room for someone, or to change a plan to suit them.
practiceSentences: The hall can accommodate the whole of Year 6 at once.
How many readers can this library accommodate?
She changed the timetable to accommodate the late bus.
A good plan can accommodate one surprise without collapsing.
Accommodate is spelled with two c's and two m's.

words.group: Spelling: double letters and silent endings
words.childMeaning: A place for someone to stay or live.
practiceSentences: The school arranged accommodation for the visiting choir.
What accommodation is there near the coast?
Accommodation near the market costs more than it did.
Finding accommodation was harder than finding the money.
Accommodation carries the same double letters as accommodate.

words.group: Spelling: double letters and silent endings
words.childMeaning: Doing something for love of it rather than for pay.
practiceSentences: An amateur photographer took the best picture of the day.
Is this an amateur competition or a professional one?
Amal plays for an amateur team and trains twice a week.
An amateur does it for love; a professional does it for a living.
The word amateur comes from the Latin for "to love".

words.group: Spelling: double letters and silent endings
words.childMeaning: Joined or fixed to something, or fond of someone.
practiceSentences: A short note was attached to the parcel.
Which document is attached to this letter?
The shed is attached to the side of the house.
Dina grew very attached to the stray cat.
Attached keeps both t's when the ending is added.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: The character whose wanting drives the story and who is changed by it.
practiceSentences: A protagonist is not simply the person on every page.
What does the protagonist of this fable actually want?
The protagonist ends the story as somebody slightly different.
Amal argued that the village, not the boy, is the real protagonist.
A story can have a protagonist you do not like at all.

words.group: Words that concede a point
words.childMeaning: Used to accept a point before making your own.
practiceSentences: Admittedly, the plan cost more than expected.
The tale is short; admittedly, it says a great deal.
Admittedly the ending is sudden, but is it the wrong ending?
She was tired, admittedly, and the work was still finished.
Admittedly concedes something before the argument continues.

words.group: Words that concede a point
words.childMeaning: Used to say something can be argued, though others may disagree.
practiceSentences: This is arguably the finest fable in the collection.
Is the second ending arguably the stronger one?
Arguably, the villagers are more at fault than the boy.
The opening is arguably too slow for a short tale.
Arguably signals a claim you are prepared to defend.

words.group: Words: devices, data and being online
words.childMeaning: Working well while wasting as little time, energy or effort as possible.
practiceSentences: A trained heart is efficient because it pumps more blood with every single beat.
An efficient warm-up prepares the whole body without wasting precious training minutes.
How can we make our team practice more efficient and far less tiring?
"Be efficient with your energy," the coach advised the runners before the long race.
I try to be efficient by finishing my homework before evening football practice.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Agreeing to something, or coming to terms with it.
practiceSentences: Her acceptance of the apology ended the quarrel.
What helps a person reach acceptance after a loss?
The club sent a letter of acceptance to every applicant.
Acceptance does not mean you agree with everything.
The fable ends in acceptance rather than revenge.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A worried, nervous feeling that arrives before something difficult.
practiceSentences: A small knot of anxiety sat in Amal's stomach as the concert began.
Taking slow, deep breaths can help you calm your anxiety before a test.
Have you ever felt anxiety before speaking in front of the whole class?
"Talking to my mum about my anxiety always makes me feel better," said Noah.
Nora's anxiety melted away when she saw her friends waving at the school gate.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Working together with other people to get something done or reach a shared goal.
practiceSentences: Good cooperation helped the team finish before the deadline.
Why does cooperation matter so much during a group project?
"Amazing cooperation, Sami!" shouted Nora as the windmill finally spun.
Teacher Yasmin praised the cooperation between every table in the hall.
The tale teaches the value of cooperation, patience and steady work.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The quality of trying hard even when something is difficult.
practiceSentences: Her fierce determination carried her through every hard mile of the charity race.
Where does such quiet determination come from when the task seems impossible?
"Determination will take you far," Sami's coach said after the exhausting training.
My own determination grew stronger each time I refused to give up on maths.
With quiet determination, Amal rewrote her speech until every line felt right.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A calm, serious manner that earns other people's respect.
practiceSentences: She accepted the result with great dignity.
How does the old woman keep her dignity in the story?
Losing well takes as much dignity as winning.
He spoke with the quiet dignity of someone sure of himself.
Every person deserves to be treated with dignity.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The habit of training yourself to follow rules and keep working hard.
practiceSentences: Great athletes need discipline as much as they need natural talent.
What kind of discipline does long-distance running actually demand?
Sami showed real discipline by practising every day before school!
Without discipline, even a talented player can fall behind.
They trained with discipline, ate well, rested properly and listened to their coaches.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The presence of many different kinds of people or things.
practiceSentences: The diversity of birds along the river surprised us.
How does diversity make a class stronger?
Our school celebrates the diversity of its families.
A forest's diversity protects it from disease.
Diversity of opinion makes a discussion worth having.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Words or actions that give someone hope and confidence.
practiceSentences: A word of encouragement from Nora changed his whole day.
Who gave you the most encouragement this year?
She needed encouragement, not correction.
The crowd's encouragement carried the runners home.
Small encouragement at the right moment goes a long way.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Choosing to stop being angry with someone who wronged you.
practiceSentences: Forgiveness took him longer than an apology would have.
Is forgiveness always the right ending to a story?
She asked for forgiveness and meant it.
The fable turns on an act of forgiveness.
Forgiveness frees the person who gives it.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A feeling of being upset or annoyed because you cannot do something you want.
practiceSentences: Amal felt a wave of frustration when the soldiers banned the peaceful gathering by the river.
Maya could not hide her frustration when the soldiers cancelled the market again.
How do you calm your frustration when a plan collapses at the last moment?
"Let go of your frustration," the elder advised, "and think clearly instead."
I felt real frustration after studying hard, yet the exam questions surprised me completely.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The quality of giving freely and kindly to others.
practiceSentences: Sami thanked his neighbour for her generosity after the storm.
Why does generosity matter so much in this old sheeko, Amal?
What generosity you showed today, Jamal!
The tale ends by praising the young boy's generosity to strangers.
A sheeko might teach generosity, or courage, or respect for elders.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A deep sadness felt after losing someone or something dear.
practiceSentences: Even grief must follow rules, the soldier told the villagers.
Could anyone truly measure the grief inside that quiet crowd?
"Your grief is real," Amal's grandmother said softly.
The grief in the village lasted long after the funeral.
Sharing memories together helped the family carry their grief.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A feeling of being unsure about yourself or your worth.
practiceSentences: His insecurity showed in the way he avoided the question.
What insecurity does the boastful lion hide?
Insecurity often sounds like showing off.
She admitted her insecurity about reading aloud.
Kindness costs little and eases another's insecurity.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A plan or purpose you have in mind before you act.
practiceSentences: Her intention was kind, even though the result was not.
What was the traveller's intention in the fable?
Judge the intention as well as the outcome.
He had every intention of returning the book.
A good intention badly carried out still causes harm.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Behaving in a sensible, grown-up way.
practiceSentences: She handled the disappointment with real maturity.
What maturity does the youngest brother show?
Maturity is not the same as age.
Admitting a mistake takes maturity.
Leo answered with a maturity that surprised everyone.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Paying calm, careful attention to the present moment.
practiceSentences: A minute of mindfulness settled the whole class.
How does mindfulness help before a test?
She practises mindfulness by noticing five sounds.
Mindfulness is noticing without judging.
The elder's mindfulness is what the sheeko admires.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A failure to understand something correctly.
practiceSentences: The whole quarrel began with one misunderstanding.
How could that misunderstanding have been avoided?
A single question would have cleared the misunderstanding.
Their misunderstanding lasted a week and cost a friendship.
Most of the fable's trouble comes from a misunderstanding.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A habit of expecting good things to happen.
practiceSentences: Her optimism kept the group going through the rain.
Is optimism useful when a plan is failing?
Optimism is not the same as ignoring a problem.
Noah faced the long walk with steady optimism.
The ending rewards the farmer's patient optimism.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Someone of the same age or position as you.
practiceSentences: A peer can explain a puzzle better than an adult sometimes.
Who is your reading peer this term?
Peer pressure is hardest to resist when you are tired.
She read her draft aloud to a peer before handing it in.
Learning from a peer works both ways.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The regard you have for your own worth.
practiceSentences: Praise for effort builds self-esteem more than praise for talent.
How does failing affect your self-esteem?
Her self-esteem grew as her reading improved.
Low self-esteem can make a kind person seem unfriendly.
Self-esteem is not the same as boasting.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Being quick to notice and care about others' feelings.
practiceSentences: She spoke with real sensitivity about his loss.
What sensitivity does the storyteller show here?
Sensitivity to a friend's mood is a kind of listening.
His sensitivity made him a thoughtful reader.
Sensitivity can be a strength, not a weakness.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A painful feeling that comes from doing something wrong.
practiceSentences: Shame kept him silent when he should have spoken.
How does the character move past his shame?
There is no shame in asking for help.
Her face burned with shame at the memory.
Shame that leads to change is not wasted.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The state of being healthy, comfortable and happy.
practiceSentences: Sleep matters more to wellbeing than most people think.
What helps your wellbeing on a hard week?
The school looks after the wellbeing of every pupil.
Wellbeing is not only about the body.
Time outdoors improves the wellbeing of the whole class.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A strong wish to achieve something important.
practiceSentences: Her ambition was to write a book of her own sheeko.
What ambition does the youngest son hold?
Ambition without patience rarely finishes anything.
His ambition grew after he met the visiting engineer.
The tale warns against ambition that forgets other people.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: An agreement where each side gives up something.
practiceSentences: They reached a compromise before the bell rang.
What compromise would settle this fairly?
A good compromise leaves nobody entirely happy.
The brothers found a compromise over the land.
Compromise is not the same as giving in.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Careful thought, or care for other people's feelings.
practiceSentences: She showed consideration by keeping her voice low.
What consideration does a good neighbour show?
After long consideration, he changed his answer.
Consideration for others costs nothing at all.
The plan deserves proper consideration before a vote.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Polite behaviour that shows respect for others.
practiceSentences: He answered every question with unfailing courtesy.
What courtesy does a guest owe a host?
Courtesy costs little and is remembered long.
She thanked the driver as a matter of courtesy.
The sheeko praises courtesy shown to a stranger.

words.group: Spelling: awkward vowels and tricky middles
words.childMeaning: Uncomfortable or a little difficult, especially with other people.
practiceSentences: There was an awkward silence after the whistle.
Was the question awkward or simply unexpected?
She found the first training session awkward and the second easy.
An awkward tackle can injure both players.
Awkward is an awkward word to spell.

words.group: Spelling: awkward vowels and tricky middles
words.childMeaning: Something bought cheaply, or an agreement about a price.
practiceSentences: The old bicycle was a real bargain.
Is that a bargain or just a low price?
They struck a bargain over the cost of the kit.
A bargain you never use has cost you everything.
Amara drove a hard bargain at the market.

words.group: Spelling: awkward vowels and tricky middles
words.childMeaning: A dark mark on the skin where it has been struck.
practiceSentences: A bruise appeared on his shin after the match.
How long does a bruise take to fade?
Ice reduces the swelling around a bruise.
A bruise is blood trapped under the skin.
Bruise rhymes with news, not with rise.

words.group: Spelling: awkward vowels and tricky middles
words.childMeaning: A public disagreement in which people take strong opposite sides.
practiceSentences: The referee's decision caused a controversy that lasted weeks.
Why is there such controversy about the new rule?
A controversy is not settled by the loudest voice.
The controversy over the stadium divided the whole town.
Controversy needs two sides who both believe they are right.

words.group: Words that match one thing to another
words.childMeaning: In a way that matches a change just described.
practiceSentences: The pitch was longer, and the match correspondingly slower.
Did the harder training bring a correspondingly better result?
Prices rose, and attendance fell correspondingly.
Correspondingly fewer injuries followed the new warm-up.
Correspondingly signals that two changes move together.

words.group: Words that match one thing to another
words.childMeaning: In a way that is clear from what can be seen.
practiceSentences: He was evidently exhausted by the final lap.
Is the ankle evidently swollen, or only sore?
Evidently the notice had never been read.
She had evidently practised the routine many times.
Evidently means the evidence shows it, not that somebody said so.

words.group: Words: air, energy and the living world
words.childMeaning: The change of a liquid into a gas as it warms.
practiceSentences: Evaporation turns the puddle into water vapour.
What causes evaporation to happen faster?
Heat from the sun speeds up evaporation.
The class measured evaporation from two dishes.
Evaporation is one step in the water cycle.

words.group: Words: air, energy and the living world
words.childMeaning: Clear enough to see straight through.
practiceSentences: The water was transparent right to the bottom.
Is that transparent lid made of glass?
Ice can be transparent or cloudy white.
A transparent bag lets you see what is inside.
Amal used a transparent jar for the experiment.

words.group: Words: air, energy and the living world
words.childMeaning: Able to be replaced or used again, like energy from the sun or the wind.
practiceSentences: Solar power is a renewable source because we can use the sun over and over again.
Amal's display promised renewable hope, planted through steady, patient action.
Why is renewable energy better for the ozone layer than burning dirty fuel?
"Wind is renewable, so it will never simply run out," the engineer told us.
I want our school to run on renewable energy from panels on the roof.

words.group: Words: air, energy and the living world
words.childMeaning: Looking after nature so it is not damaged or used up.
practiceSentences: Conservation protects the forest and its animals.
What can our class do for conservation?
Water conservation matters in a dry season.
The park has a conservation area for birds.
Nora joined a conservation club after school.

words.group: Words: air, energy and the living world
words.childMeaning: A community of living things and their surroundings that all depend on each other.
practiceSentences: The forest is an ecosystem where plants, animals and insects all help one another.
"If the forest keeps drying out, the whole ecosystem will collapse," warned Doctor Alina.
How does removing one animal change the balance of an entire ecosystem?
"An ecosystem is a web, not a list," Teacher Yasmin said, drawing the links on the board.
I learned that a healthy ecosystem gives us clean air, water and food.

words.group: Words: air, energy and the living world
words.childMeaning: Close to the real amount, but not exact.
practiceSentences: Give me an approximate depth of the lake.
Is that an approximate or an exact figure?
The approximate temperature was twenty degrees.
An approximate answer is enough for this task.
Sami wrote the approximate weight in his notes.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The study of stars, planets and everything else in space.
practiceSentences: People have studied astronomy since ancient times, long before telescopes existed.
Why does astronomy interest so many young scientists today?
Sami joined the astronomy club to learn more about the planets.
Modern astronomy relies on powerful telescopes and orbiting satellites.
Astronomy asks questions that take centuries to answer.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.
practiceSentences: Everything around you is built from atoms.
How small is a single atom?
An atom has a nucleus with electrons around it.
Two atoms of hydrogen join one of oxygen to make water.
No microscope can show you a single atom directly.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A huge group of stars, dust and gas held together in space.
practiceSentences: Our sun is one star in a galaxy of billions.
Which galaxy is nearest to our own?
A galaxy can take shapes like a spiral or a disc.
Light from a distant galaxy takes millions of years.
Sami drew the shape of our galaxy from memory.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The curved path one object takes around another in space.
practiceSentences: The moon completes its orbit in about a month.
How long is the orbit of this satellite?
The rockets that carry satellites into orbit are marvels of engineering.
Earth's orbit around the sun takes a year.
A lower orbit means a faster journey round.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A satellite is a machine sent into space that circles the Earth and sends back information.
practiceSentences: The satellite picture showed the cyclone spinning slowly over the ocean.
How does a satellite send weather pictures back down to Earth?
Sami, did you see the satellite image the news showed of the storm?
Scientists used the satellite to track exactly where the cyclone would land.
A weather satellite passes over the island several times a day.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: Relating to or powered by energy from the sun.
practiceSentences: A solar panel can collect enough energy to charge a phone by evening.
How much power can a small solar charger really produce?
Omar, this solar jar keeps glowing long after sunset!
Families without electricity often depend on solar power instead.
The solar panel collects energy and stores it in the battery.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: Everything that exists: all space, matter and time.
practiceSentences: The universe is far larger than anyone can picture.
How old is the universe thought to be?
Our galaxy is a very small part of the universe.
The universe is still expanding today.
Talia asked whether the universe has an edge.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: Energy that travels out from a source as heat, light or invisible rays.
practiceSentences: The sun gives off radiation that warms the Earth and lets green plants grow.
New funding went to clean-up crews and to safe radiation containment near the grove.
How do astronauts shield themselves from the harmful radiation found in outer space?
"Too much radiation from the sun can burn your skin," the doctor reminded us.
I learned that the ozone layer blocks a lot of harmful radiation from the sun.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: Light or sound bouncing back off a surface.
practiceSentences: She saw her reflection in the still water.
What causes the reflection you see in a window?
A mirror works by reflection of light.
The reflection of the moon lay across the lake.
Sound bounces back too, and we call that reflection.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A basic element found in all living things and in materials like coal and diamonds.
practiceSentences: Green plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and use it to build their leaves.
Green plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and use it to grow.
Why does burning too much fuel release harmful carbon into our atmosphere?
"Trees store carbon," the ranger explained, "which keeps our air cleaner."
I learned that reducing carbon emissions helps protect the fragile natural world.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A compound is a substance made when two or more elements join together.
practiceSentences: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Which compound gives the sea its salty taste?
The scientists heated the compound until it changed colour.
Salt is a common compound found in every kitchen.
A compound can behave very differently from the elements inside it.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A group of atoms joined together as one unit.
practiceSentences: A water molecule has three atoms.
How many atoms are in this molecule?
Molecules move faster when they are heated.
A single molecule is far too small to see.
Leo built a model of a molecule from clay and sticks.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The hot gas water turns into when it boils.
practiceSentences: If you lift the lid too early, the steam escapes.
What makes the steam rise from the kettle?
Steam turned the wheels of the earliest engines.
Steam is invisible until it cools into tiny droplets.
The steam clouded the cold window.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A sour substance that can burn or dissolve other materials.
practiceSentences: Lemon juice is a weak acid.
Which acid is used in a car battery?
Strong acid must be handled with gloves.
Acid rain wears away stone over many years.
The class tested each liquid to find the acid.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The change from a gas back into a liquid as it cools.
practiceSentences: Condensation forms on a cold glass on a warm day.
What causes the condensation on the window?
Clouds form by condensation high in the air.
Condensation is the opposite of evaporation.
Wipe the condensation away before you read the scale.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: How often something happens in a given time.
practiceSentences: The frequency of the signal decides its pitch.
What is the frequency of these readings?
A higher frequency means more waves each second.
Storms rose in frequency over the decade.
Radios pick out one frequency from many.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: Related to electricity or using electricity.
practiceSentences: The engineer checked the electrical wiring carefully before switching on the new machine.
Why must electrical equipment be handled so cautiously to avoid dangerous shocks?
"Never touch electrical cables," the teacher warned, "especially when your hands are wet."
I learned that electrical energy powers almost every device we use each day.
The electrician tested every electrical socket in the new classrooms.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A room fitted out for science experiments.
practiceSentences: The samples are kept in the laboratory fridge.
What rules apply in the laboratory?
A laboratory needs good light and running water.
She works in a laboratory studying soil.
Wear goggles whenever you enter the laboratory.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The slow change of living things over very long periods.
practiceSentences: Evolution explains why species differ from one another.
How does evolution happen so slowly?
Fossils give us evidence of evolution.
Evolution works over millions of years, not lifetimes.
The museum's display traces the evolution of the horse.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago.
practiceSentences: The fossil was found deep in the cliff face.
How old is this fossil thought to be?
A fossil can be a bone, a shell or a footprint.
Each fossil is a record of a living thing.
Zara cleaned the fossil with a soft brush.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: A feature that helps a living thing survive where it lives.
practiceSentences: Thick fur is an adaptation to a cold climate.
Which adaptation helps this plant hold water?
Every adaptation has a cost as well as a use.
The camel's foot is an adaptation to soft sand.
Adaptation happens over generations, not in one life.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
practiceSentences: The owl is a predator that hunts at night.
Which predator hunts here after dark?
A predator keeps the numbers of its prey in check.
Removing a predator can upset a whole habitat.
The cheetah is the fastest predator on land.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
practiceSentences: The lion crept low, watching its prey across the grass.
How does a cheetah catch prey that can run so fast?
Nora held her breath as the prey darted away just in time!
Every predator on the savannah depends on finding enough prey.
An owl hunts its prey silently in the dark.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The wearing away of soil or rock by wind, water or ice.
practiceSentences: Erosion has cut a deep valley through the rock.
What causes erosion along this coast?
Tree roots slow erosion on a steep slope.
Erosion works over centuries, grain by grain.
The cliff path was closed because of erosion.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The breaking down of rock where it lies, by weather.
practiceSentences: Weathering cracks the rock before erosion carries it off.
How does frost cause weathering?
Weathering happens in place; erosion moves the pieces.
The statue's face was blurred by weathering.
Chemical weathering slowly dissolves limestone.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The height of something above sea level or ground level.
practiceSentences: At such a high altitude, the thin air made every climber breathe much harder.
Why does the temperature drop as the altitude of a mountain increases?
"We are gaining altitude," the pilot announced, "so please fasten your seatbelts now."
I felt dizzy at high altitude, where the mountain air seemed strangely thin.
The village sits at an altitude of two thousand metres.

words.group: Spelling: -ous, -ity and doubled consonants
words.childMeaning: A strong wish to learn or find out about something.
practiceSentences: Curiosity is what keeps a field biologist watching for hours.
What first stirred your curiosity about wild animals?
Curiosity killed the cat, but it also wrote every field guide.
Her curiosity about the nest cost her a whole afternoon.
Curiosity asks the question; patience answers it.

words.group: Spelling: -ous, -ity and doubled consonants
words.childMeaning: Causing very great harm or damage.
practiceSentences: Clearing the forest had disastrous effects on the river.
Why was that season so disastrous for the herd?
A disastrous drought can empty a valley in months.
Introducing one new species proved disastrous for the rest.
Disastrous keeps the o of disaster and loses the e.

words.group: Spelling: -ous, -ity and doubled consonants
words.childMeaning: Supplied with what is needed for a task.
practiceSentences: The team arrived well equipped for a week in the bush.
Is the camp equipped for the rainy season?
A camel is equipped for heat in ways a horse is not.
They equipped every ranger with a radio.
Equipped doubles the p before the ending.

words.group: Spelling: -ous, -ity and doubled consonants
words.childMeaning: To bother or annoy someone repeatedly.
practiceSentences: Tourists who harass an animal change how it behaves.
Why do smaller birds harass a hawk?
Do not harass a nesting bird for a photograph.
The rangers stop visitors who harass the elephants.
Harass has one r and two s's, which trips most people.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: A series of things where each is linked to the next.
practiceSentences: A food chain shows which living thing eats which.
Where does this chain begin?
Remove one species and the whole chain can fall apart.
Every food chain starts with a plant and ends with a decomposer.
Amara drew the chain from grass to zebra to lion.

words.group: Words that carry an idea forward
words.childMeaning: From this time onwards.
practiceSentences: Henceforth the reserve will be closed to vehicles.
Will the rule apply henceforth, or from next year?
The species was henceforth protected by law.
Henceforth all sightings must be recorded on the same form.
Henceforth looks forward; hitherto looks back.

words.group: Words that carry an idea forward
words.childMeaning: To the extent that; because of the fact that.
practiceSentences: The plan succeeded inasmuch as the herd survived.
Is it a success inasmuch as anything was saved?

words.group: Words: the body, food and staying well

words.group: Words: the body, food and staying well

words.group: Words: the body, food and staying well

words.group: Words: the body, food and staying well

words.group: Words: the body, food and staying well

words.group: Words: the body, food and staying well

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

Nobody doubted Zara's trustworthiness.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Good enough for what is needed, but no more.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Having a strong wish to achieve something difficult.
practiceSentences: The plan was ambitious for a class of ten.

An ambitious project needs an honest timetable.
Daniel set himself an ambitious reading goal.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Made by people rather than grown or formed in nature.

Maya's science project compared natural light with artificial light for growing beans.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Happening by itself, without a person having to make it happen each time.

Maya, that response felt completely automatic, like you had practised it!
The sprinklers turn on at an automatic time every morning.
The camera has an automatic flash for dark rooms.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Large enough to matter; a good deal of something.
practiceSentences: A considerable amount of rain fell overnight.
Was there considerable damage to the roof?
She showed considerable patience with the beginners.
The task took considerable time and care.
Considerable effort went into the display.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Always behaving or happening in the same way.
practiceSentences: Her handwriting is consistent from start to finish.
Are the readings consistent with yesterday's?
Consistent practice beats occasional bursts.
The rule must be consistent for everyone.
His story stayed consistent under questioning.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Helpful, and meant to improve rather than to knock down.
practiceSentences: Her comments were constructive and easy to use.
What makes criticism constructive?
A constructive suggestion offers a way forward.
Be constructive, even when you disagree.
The meeting was short but constructive.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Good enough at explaining something to make you believe it.
practiceSentences: Her argument was clear and convincing.
Was the evidence convincing enough?
A convincing story keeps its details straight.
He gave a convincing account of what happened.
The excuse was not remotely convincing.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Very important or necessary.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Made up of many different kinds.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: To do with the home, or with your own country.
practiceSentences: Domestic chores were shared between them all.

Domestic news filled the first three pages.
She wrote about domestic life in the 1950s.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Sudden and striking, or to do with plays.
practiceSentences: There was a dramatic change in the weather.

A dramatic pause can be worth a paragraph.
The dramatic society meets on Tuesdays.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Helping people to learn something.
practiceSentences: The trip was enjoyable and genuinely educational.

The museum runs educational visits for schools.
She found the whole experience educational.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Connected to the natural world and how human actions affect it.
practiceSentences: We should protect our environmental resources, such as clean water and healthy trees.

What environmental conditions make it dangerous for athletes to train outside?

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

practiceSentences: Her memory for dates is exceptional.

An exceptional result deserves an explanation.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: On or from the outside.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

Gradual progress is still progress.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: The best or most perfect for a purpose.
practiceSentences: Soft morning light is ideal for photographing birds.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

The waterfall is impressive after heavy rain.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully

words.group: Spelling: French endings and silent letters

words.group: Spelling: French endings and silent letters

words.group: Spelling: French endings and silent letters
words.childMeaning: Something or someone that causes trouble or annoyance.

Nuisance ends in -ance, not -ence.

words.group: Spelling: French endings and silent letters

Tasks wait in a queue until the processor is free.
Queue is one letter followed by four that say nothing.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others

Two readers may interpret a story differently.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others
words.childMeaning: To convince someone to do or believe something by giving good reasons.

words.childMeaning: To give a short account of the main points.

Summarise the chapter in your own words.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others
words.childMeaning: The difference between two things when you compare them.

What contrast did you notice in the photographs?

Note the contrast between the two endings.
Nora described the contrast in one clear sentence.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others
words.childMeaning: To finish something, or to decide after thinking.

What did the class conclude from the survey?

Leo tried to conclude his speech with a question.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others
words.childMeaning: To give good reasons for something.
practiceSentences: Can you justify your answer with evidence?

Justify your opinion before others reply.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others
words.childMeaning: To work out something from clues rather than being told.

Infer the reason before you check the last page.

Cite the author's name and the page number.

words.group: Words: rights, fairness and telling others

words.childMeaning: A list of the books and sources used in a piece of work.

Nothing in the tale turns out to be permanent.

words.group: Words: how a story is built

words.group: Words: how a story is built

words.group: Words: how a story is built

words.group: Words: how a story is built

words.group: Words: how a story is built

Pupils were asked to contribute questions before the courtroom visit.
Everyone can contribute an idea, however small it seems.

words.group: Words: doing, trying and finding out
words.childMeaning: To succeed in doing something you set out to do.
practiceSentences: The team hoped to accomplish the task by noon.
What did you accomplish this week?
Hard work helps you accomplish your goal.
Leo accomplished more than he expected.
They accomplished the climb in three hours.

words.group: Words: doing, trying and finding out
words.childMeaning: To show clearly how something works.
practiceSentences: Leo will demonstrate the experiment to us.
Can you demonstrate the correct grip?
The coach demonstrated the throw twice.
These results demonstrate that the plan works.
Demonstrate the step slowly for beginners.

words.group: Words: doing, trying and finding out
words.childMeaning: To find out or decide something after thinking about it.
practiceSentences: We must determine which route is shorter.
How will you determine the winner?
Tests determine how strong the material is.
The weather will determine our starting time.
Nora tried to determine the cause of the fault.

words.group: Words: doing, trying and finding out
words.childMeaning: To judge how good or useful something is.
practiceSentences: Evaluate your plan before you begin.
How will you evaluate the results?
The class will evaluate each design fairly.
Nora took time to evaluate both options.
Evaluate the evidence before you decide.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To admit that something is true.
practiceSentences: She was willing to acknowledge her mistake.
Will he acknowledge that the plan has failed?
Good writing acknowledges the other side of an argument.
He would not acknowledge that anything was wrong.
Acknowledge the source of every fact you borrow.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To expect something and get ready for it.
practiceSentences: Good planning anticipates what could go wrong.
Did anyone anticipate this much rain?
She learned to anticipate the questions she would be asked.
A driver must anticipate what other cars will do.
We anticipate finishing before Friday.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To believe something is true without having full proof of it.
practiceSentences: Amal warned her classmate never to assume too much from one piece of evidence.
Why do people so often assume the worst without any proof?
Do not assume the answer before you check!
A careful judge will never assume anything before hearing every witness.
We should never assume that tomorrow will look exactly like today.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To make something clearer or easier to understand.
practiceSentences: Could you clarify the second instruction?
What would clarify this diagram?
One example can clarify a whole paragraph.
She rewrote the notice to clarify the times.
Ask a question if you need to clarify anything.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To work together with others on the same task.
practiceSentences: Two classes will collaborate on the display.
Why collaborate rather than work alone?
Scientists collaborate across many countries.
They collaborate best when the roles are clear.
Nora and Kobi collaborate on the class newsletter.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To understand something fully.
practiceSentences: It is hard to comprehend a number that large.
Do you comprehend what the rule actually asks?
Reading twice helps you comprehend the argument.
She could not comprehend his reasoning at first.
To comprehend is more than to recognise the words.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To carry out or organise an activity.
practiceSentences: Scientists conduct careful tests before every launch.
Why do astronauts conduct so many experiments in space?
Nora and Sami conduct a small experiment each week.
The crew must conduct repairs quickly if something breaks.
She will conduct the interview herself.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To ask someone for advice or information.
practiceSentences: Consult the timetable before you set out.
Who would you consult about this?
She consults a dictionary whenever she is unsure.
They consulted the elders before deciding.
Consult more than one source for a fact that matters.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To notice or find something that is hidden or hard to see.
practiceSentences: The visitor praised the students for learning to detect meaning in symbols.
Trained dogs can detect scents that humans would never notice.
Can you detect the tiny spelling mistake hidden in this sentence?
'Smoke alarms detect danger long before we smell anything,' said the firefighter.
Using a magnifying glass, I tried to detect fingerprints on the glass.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To tell the difference between two things.
practiceSentences: Can you distinguish a fact from an opinion?
How do you distinguish these two birds?
Colour alone will not distinguish the samples.
It is hard to distinguish the twins by voice.
Learn to distinguish evidence from assertion.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To make something seem important by saying it clearly or strongly.
practiceSentences: Underlining a word is one simple way to emphasise it on the page.
Our teacher used a red marker to emphasise the most important dates.
Why did the author emphasise the storm at the beginning of the chapter?
'Please emphasise the first word when you read the title,' said Teacher Yasmin.
When I practised my speech, I tried to emphasise the parts about teamwork.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To create or start something meant to last.
practiceSentences: They hope to establish a library in the village.
When was the school established?
The study established a clear link between the two.
She established a routine and kept to it.
First establish the facts, then argue from them.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To produce or create something.
practiceSentences: Wind turbines generate electricity.
How much power does this panel generate?
The topic generated more debate than expected.
They generate new ideas by working in pairs.
Heat is generated whenever the parts rub.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To describe the main points without the detail.
practiceSentences: Outline your argument in five bullet points.
Can you outline the plan in one minute?
She outlined the story before writing a word.
The letter outlines what happens next.
An outline is a skeleton, not a draft.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To suggest an idea or plan for others to think about.
practiceSentences: The engineer stood up to propose a bold plan for cleaner city transport.
May I propose a simpler design that uses far fewer materials?
"I propose we test the prototype today," Maya suggested to the excited team.
I decided to propose a recycling scheme to improve our busy school playground.
'We propose an open science zone,' they wrote.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To think carefully about something, or to give back an image of it.
practiceSentences: After the difficult exam, take a moment to reflect on what you might improve.
Do these results truly reflect the effort you put into your project?
"Let us reflect on our grandparents' advice," the teacher said gently to the children.
Every evening I pause to reflect on my choices and give thanks for the day.
Still water can reflect the mountains like a mirror.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To resolve means to find an answer to a problem or bring a disagreement to an end.
practiceSentences: The two friends met after school to resolve their argument.
How did the committee resolve the dispute over the water pump?
Talking honestly is the quickest way to resolve a misunderstanding.
The referee stepped in to resolve the confusion over the score.
Amal helped the younger pupils resolve their quarrel fairly.

words.group: Spelling: -ment, -ation and -ive
words.childMeaning: A notice or message made to persuade people to buy or support something.
practiceSentences: The advertisement promised more than the product delivered.
Which advertisement persuaded you, and how?
An advertisement is written to be believed, not to be true.
She placed an advertisement for a cleaner in the paper.
Advertisement keeps the e of advertise in the middle.

words.group: Spelling: -ment, -ation and -ive
words.childMeaning: The building of a case out of reasons and evidence.
practiceSentences: Careful argumentation matters more than a loud voice.
What makes argumentation persuasive rather than merely long?
Good argumentation answers the strongest objection, not the weakest.
Her argumentation moved from evidence to conclusion in three steps.
Argumentation is the method; an argument is one instance of it.

words.group: Spelling: -ment, -ation and -ive
words.childMeaning: The sorting of things into groups by what they have in common.
practiceSentences: Job classification decides which rules apply to a worker.
What classification does this role fall under?
A classification is useful only if the groups do not overlap.
The library's classification puts every book in one place.
Classification asks what things share, not what they are called.

words.group: Spelling: -ment, -ation and -ive
words.childMeaning: A word that joins ideas and shows how they relate.
practiceSentences: The word "however" is a connective that signals a contrast.
Which connective would join these two sentences?
A connective tells the reader what to expect next.
Her writing improved when she varied her connectives.
A connective joins ideas; a conjunction joins clauses.

words.group: Words that draw a conclusion
words.childMeaning: For that reason; in this way.
practiceSentences: The road flooded; thus the market was cancelled.
Is the conclusion thus proved, or only suggested?
Thus the two departments came to share a budget.
She missed the deadline and thus lost the contract.
Thus is a formal way of saying "so", and takes a semicolon before it.

words.group: Words that draw a conclusion
words.childMeaning: Certainly, with no room for doubt.
practiceSentences: The reform undoubtedly helped the poorest families.
Is that undoubtedly true, or merely likely?
Undoubtedly the scheme cost more than was promised.
She is undoubtedly the best candidate for the post.
Undoubtedly claims certainty, so it should be used sparingly.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: The power to make decisions, or a group that holds it.
practiceSentences: The head teacher has authority over the school.
Which authority looks after our local roads?
A police officer has authority to stop traffic.
She spoke with quiet authority.
The local authority repaired the broken bridge.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A person who is trying to be chosen for a position, such as in an election.
practiceSentences: Amal became a candidate for dormitory representative last term.
Which candidate do you think gave the strongest speech today?
Good luck, Nora, our newest candidate for class president!
Every candidate stood nervously at the front of the hall.
Each candidate had to give a short talk.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A person who works with you at your job.
practiceSentences: My mother met a colleague at the market.
Is he a colleague of your father?
A good colleague shares the work fairly.
Teacher Yasmin thanked a colleague for the help.
The nurse asked a colleague to check the notes.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A person who buys or uses things.
practiceSentences: Every consumer should read the label before paying at the till.
A smart consumer compares prices before buying anything.
What should a consumer check on a food label?
"Every consumer has the right to complain," said the shopkeeper.
I became a careful consumer after wasting my pocket money once.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A person who moves to live in another country.
practiceSentences: An immigrant learns new streets, new words, and new friends.
The immigrant doctor learned the local language very quickly.
What challenges does an immigrant face in a new country?
"My grandfather arrived as an immigrant with one suitcase," said Father.
Our class heard an immigrant tell her brave journey story.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A person or animal that lives in a place.
practiceSentences: Every inhabitant of the village knew the story.
How many inhabitants does the town have?
The island has fewer than fifty inhabitants.
The owl is an inhabitant of the deep forest.
Each inhabitant was asked to join the clean-up.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A smaller group within a much larger one.
practiceSentences: Only a minority voted against the plan.
Which minority language is spoken here?
A minority of pupils travel by bus.
The rights of every minority must be protected.
Nora spoke up for the minority view.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A person who is walking, especially in a street.
practiceSentences: A pedestrian must use the crossing.
Is there a safe path for every pedestrian?
The pedestrian waited for the green light.
Drivers should watch for a pedestrian at night.
The new pedestrian bridge opened last week.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A system where people vote to choose their leaders.
practiceSentences: In a democracy, every adult may vote.
How does democracy protect people's rights?
Our class council is a small democracy.
Democracy needs everyone to take part.
The country returned to democracy after years.

words.group: Words: work, law and taking part
words.childMeaning: A set of rules that explains how a country or group works.
practiceSentences: Our club's constitution gives every member a vote.
Who wrote the country's first constitution?
The constitution protects the rights of citizens.
The council wrote a short constitution.
Changing a constitution takes a long time.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A retelling of events in the order they happened.
practiceSentences: Her recount of the trip filled two pages.
Is this a recount or a story?
A recount keeps to what actually happened.
Write a recount of the sports day for the newsletter.
A recount uses the past tense throughout.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Not formal or official; relaxed and casual.
practiceSentences: An informal note to a friend can begin with hello rather than dear.
The rangers held an informal meeting around the campfire.
Is it acceptable to use informal language in a letter to the mayor?
"Keep the interview informal so the children relax," said the director.
Our informal kickabout in the park turned into a proper match.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A piece of writing that argues or explains one idea.
practiceSentences: Her essay argued for a longer school library slot.
How many paragraphs should this essay have?
An essay needs one idea, not five.
He planned the essay before writing a word.
The best essay in the class was also the shortest.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Writing that sets out to argue for a point of view.
practiceSentences: An argumentative essay states a claim and defends it.
What makes this piece argumentative rather than informative?
Argumentative writing must answer the other side.
She chose an argumentative form for the topic.
The argumentative structure suits a debate.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A careful judgement of how good or useful something is.
practiceSentences: Her evaluation of the two methods was fair.
What evaluation would you give this design?
An evaluation weighs strengths against weaknesses.
The evaluation goes at the end of the report.
A good evaluation gives reasons, not verdicts.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Meaning exactly what the words say, with nothing figurative.
practiceSentences: Take the instruction in its literal sense.
Is that a literal description or an image?
A literal translation can miss the meaning entirely.
"Raining cats and dogs" is not literal.
The literal meaning and the intended one differ here.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A hook is an exciting opening that grabs the reader's attention.
practiceSentences: A strong hook makes the reader want to know what happens next.
Which hook works better, a question or a surprising fact?
Maya's hook was a single mysterious sentence about a locked door.
Start your article with a hook before you give the details.
The best hook leaves the reader with a question they must answer.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: To state something exactly and clearly.
practiceSentences: Please specify which edition you mean.
Did the instructions specify a time?
She specified the exact measurements.
The rules do not specify how many may enter.
Specify the source, not just the claim.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: To change something into a different form or appearance.
practiceSentences: A tiny seed can transform into a towering tree given water, soil, and sunlight.
How can reading widely transform the way a young person understands the world?
"Hard work will transform your grades," the teacher promised, "if you stay patient and focused."
I hope to transform our dull playground into a bright, welcoming garden.
Art, music and creative expression can transform communities and inspire change.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: The only one of its kind.
practiceSentences: Every genre has its own unique features, which is how readers tell them apart.
Every snowflake has a unique pattern that no other snowflake shares.
What makes your fingerprint unique compared with everyone else's?
"Each of you has a unique talent," our head teacher reminded the assembly.
I keep a unique spiral shell on my shelf that I found on holiday.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: True or shared everywhere, by everyone.
practiceSentences: Grief is a universal human experience.
Is that rule universal, or local to us?
The story's appeal is universal.
Some symbols are close to universal.
A universal claim is the hardest kind to prove.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Not expected to happen or be true; improbable.
practiceSentences: It seems unlikely that the well will fill again before winter.
Is it unlikely that Zara remembers every word she has heard?
What an unlikely ending to such a strange story!
Jamal thought rain was unlikely, but the sky soon turned grey.
Storytellers add unlikely details until the tale outgrows the truth.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Well founded, and able to stand up to examination.
practiceSentences: That is a valid objection and deserves an answer.
Is the argument still valid without this evidence?
A valid ticket must show today's date.
Her reasoning was valid even where I disagreed.
One weak step makes the whole proof less valid.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Extremely large in size or amount.
practiceSentences: A vast plain stretched to the horizon.
How vast is the desert to the north?
There is a vast difference between the two drafts.
The library holds a vast collection of maps.
Vast is a stronger word than big, and rarer.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Absolutely necessary for something to work or survive.
practiceSentences: Water is vital to every living thing.
Why is this step vital to the argument?
A vital piece of evidence was missing.
Sleep is vital, not a luxury.
The vital question is who benefits.

words.group: Spelling: -or, -ency and -ive
words.childMeaning: The person who makes or invents something.
practiceSentences: The creator of the design never patented it.
Who was the creator of this map?
A creator is often remembered for one work and forgotten for the rest.
She is the creator of the school's weather station.
Creator takes -or, not -er.

words.group: Spelling: -or, -ency and -ive
words.childMeaning: The state of relying on something else.
practiceSentences: The valley's dependency on one river is a risk.
What dependency does this design have?
A dependency you cannot see is the dangerous kind.
Their dependency on imported fuel rose every year.
A dependency is what you would miss if it disappeared.

words.group: Spelling: -or, -ency and -ive
words.childMeaning: Giving a clear picture of what something is like.
practiceSentences: Her descriptive writing put us on the mountainside.
What descriptive detail would help here?
Descriptive writing shows; explanatory writing tells.
The report was descriptive but drew no conclusion.
Describe ends in -be, but descriptive has a p and a t.

words.group: Spelling: -or, -ency and -ive
words.childMeaning: The process of growing or improving something.
practiceSentences: The development of the delta took ten thousand years.
What development would you expect next?
Development is slow, and then it is sudden.
The town's development followed the road exactly.
Development also means a plot of new buildings.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A substance burned to release energy.
practiceSentences: Wood was the only fuel available in the valley.
Which fuel gives the most heat for its weight?
A fuel stores energy that burning releases.
The engine ran until the fuel was spent.
Fuel is also what keeps an argument going.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: How much mass is packed into a given space.
practiceSentences: Oil floats because its density is lower than water's.
What is the population density of this district?
Warm air rises because heating lowers its density.
Density explains why the layers in the jar never mix.
Density is mass divided by volume, and nothing else.

words.group: Words that stand in for a choice or a person
words.childMeaning: Any one of the choices, no matter which.
practiceSentences: Take whichever route is shorter today.
Whichever shape you choose, measure it twice.
Does it matter whichever door we use?
She would be pleased with whichever result came first.
Whichever narrows a choice; whatever leaves it open.

words.group: Words that stand in for a choice or a person
words.childMeaning: The form of "who" used when the person is the object.
practiceSentences: To whom should the report be addressed?
Whom did the committee choose in the end?
The engineer whom they consulted had built three dams.
Ask for whom the measurement was taken.
Use whom after a preposition: to whom, for whom, with whom.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: Understanding how another person feels.
practiceSentences: Empathy helps you comfort a sad friend.
Why does empathy matter in a team?
She listened with real empathy.
Reading stories can build empathy.
Empathy means imagining another person's day.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: The feeling of being thankful for something.
practiceSentences: She wrote a note of gratitude to her teacher.
How do you show gratitude to your family?
Gratitude costs nothing and means a great deal.
His gratitude was clear in every word.
The class expressed gratitude to the helpers.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: The reason that makes you want to do something.
practiceSentences: Her motivation was to help her family.
What is your motivation for joining the club?
Motivation fades when a task feels pointless.
A clear goal gives you motivation.
Leo found new motivation after the coach's talk.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: Being someone that others can depend on.
practiceSentences: Her reliability made her the obvious choice.
Why does reliability matter in a team?
The reliability of the old bus is poor.
Leo is known for his reliability.
Reliability is built by keeping small promises.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: Caring about someone else's sadness or difficulty.
practiceSentences: She felt sympathy for the injured bird.
Who showed sympathy when you were unwell?
A word of sympathy can help a great deal.
The class sent sympathy to the family.
Sympathy is not the same as pity.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: Accepting people whose ideas or ways differ from yours.
practiceSentences: Tolerance helps a class work well together.
Why is tolerance important in a big city?
She showed tolerance when others disagreed.
Tolerance does not mean agreeing with everything.
The school teaches tolerance and respect.

words.group: Words: character, feelings and who I am
words.childMeaning: Who a person is, and what makes them themselves.
practiceSentences: Her language is part of her identity.
What makes up your identity?
Moving country can change a person's identity.
The club gave him a sense of identity.
Identity is built from family, place and choice.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: Maths that uses letters to stand for unknown numbers.
practiceSentences: In algebra, x can stand for any number.
Why does algebra use letters instead of numbers?
Algebra lets you write a rule that always works.
She solved the algebra question in two lines.
Algebra begins where arithmetic stops.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A chart that uses pictures to stand for numbers.
practiceSentences: Each book on the pictogram stands for five readers.
What does one symbol represent on this pictogram?
A pictogram needs a key or it means nothing.
The class made a pictogram of favourite fruits.
Half a picture on a pictogram means half the value.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: The distance all the way around a circle.
practiceSentences: Measure the circumference with a piece of string.
What is the circumference of this wheel?
The circumference grows as the radius grows.
She calculated the circumference from the diameter.
A circle's circumference is a little over three diameters.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A number written with a point, such as 3.75.
practiceSentences: Write the fraction as a decimal.
Which decimal is larger, 0.7 or 0.65?
A decimal point separates whole from part.
Money is written as a decimal in most countries.
She rounded the decimal to two places.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A statement that two amounts are equal.
practiceSentences: An equation always has an equals sign.
Can you solve this equation for x?
Both sides of an equation must balance.
She checked the equation by putting the answer back.
One equation cannot give you two unknowns.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A number that divides exactly into another number.
practiceSentences: Three is a factor of twelve.
Which factors does eighteen have?
Every number has one and itself as factors.
List the factors before you look for a common one.
A prime number has exactly two factors.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A grid is a set of lines that cross to make equal squares, used in maps and maths.
practiceSentences: Plot the points on the grid before you draw the line.
Which square of the grid holds the treasure on the map?
The city's streets are laid out in a neat grid.
Use the grid to copy the drawing square by square.
Each square on the grid stands for one kilometre.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: The average found by adding values and dividing by how many.
practiceSentences: Add the five scores and divide to find the mean.
What is the mean of these numbers?
The mean can be pulled about by one extreme value.
The mean and the median are not the same thing.
She reported the mean rainfall for each month.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: The middle value when the numbers are put in order.
practiceSentences: Put the values in order, then find the median.
What is the median of this set?
The median ignores how extreme the ends are.
With an even number of values, the median is the middle two averaged.
The median often describes a group better than the mean.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A number you get by multiplying another number.
practiceSentences: Twelve is a multiple of three.
Which multiples of four are under thirty?
Every number is a multiple of one.
A common multiple appears in both times tables.
Factors divide into it; multiples come out of it.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A part of a whole expressed out of a hundred.
practiceSentences: What percentage of the class walks to school?
How do you turn a fraction into a percentage?
A percentage always compares to one hundred.
The percentage rose from twelve to twenty.
Fifty per cent is a percentage and also a half.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A flat shape with three or more straight sides.
practiceSentences: A triangle is the simplest polygon.
How many sides does this polygon have?
A circle is not a polygon.
A regular polygon has equal sides and angles.
She named every polygon on the sheet.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A number divisible only by itself and one.
practiceSentences: Seven is a prime number.
Which prime numbers are under twenty?
A prime has exactly two factors.
One is not prime, because it has only one factor.
Every whole number breaks down into primes.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: How likely something is to happen.
practiceSentences: The probability of heads is one half.
What is the probability of rain today?
A probability of zero means it cannot happen.
Probability is written as a fraction or a decimal.
High probability is not the same as certainty.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A comparison showing how much of one thing there is to another.
practiceSentences: The ratio of boys to girls is three to four.
What ratio of water to flour does the recipe need?
A ratio can be simplified like a fraction.
The map uses a ratio of one to fifty thousand.
Two to one is a ratio, not a fraction.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: Numbers collected about something, and the study of them.
practiceSentences: The statistics show a steady rise in readers.
What do these statistics actually prove?
Statistics can mislead if the sample is small.
She gathered statistics on journeys to school.
Good statistics need an honest question first.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: Something that can change, or a letter standing for it.
practiceSentences: In this equation, x is the variable.
Which variable did you change in the test?
Keep every other variable the same.
A variable can take many values.
Temperature was the variable they measured.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: An angle smaller than a right angle.
practiceSentences: An acute angle is less than ninety degrees.
Which of these angles is acute?
A triangle can have three acute angles.
The roof met the wall at an acute angle.
Acute is sharp; obtuse is blunt.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet.
