words.childMeaning: Existing on a computer rather than in the real world.
practiceSentences: They held a virtual meeting across three countries.
Is this a virtual tour or a real one?
A virtual model can be tested safely.
The museum built a virtual copy of the room.
Virtual is not the same as imaginary.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: Working without wires, by sending signals through the air.
practiceSentences: The wireless connection reaches the far classroom.
Is the printer wireless?
A wireless signal weakens through thick walls.
Wireless headphones need charging.
The whole building went wireless last year.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: The ability to enter or use something.
practiceSentences: Every pupil now has access to the library's growing collection of digital books.
Why should clean water be something everyone can access, not just the wealthy?
'You need a password to access the computer,' the librarian reminded the new students.
I felt grateful for the access to education that my parents worked so hard to provide.
They did not need expensive equipment or access to a fancy studio.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: A spare copy kept in case the original is lost.
practiceSentences: Keep a backup of your work somewhere else.
When was the last backup made?
A backup you have never tested is a hope.
The backup saved a term's worth of writing.
She makes a backup every Friday.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: A link that joins two things or lets them communicate.
practiceSentences: The connection dropped in the middle of the call.
What connection is there between the two events?
A loose connection stopped the whole circuit.
She checked every connection before switching on.
The connection between reading and writing is close.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: The way something is arranged or the kind of file it is.
practiceSentences: Save the picture in a smaller format.
Which format does the printer accept?
The report follows a set format.
She changed the format to fit one page.
A format that suits a screen may not suit paper.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: To put a program or a piece of equipment in place ready to use.
practiceSentences: Install the update before you restart.
How long does it take to install?
They installed a new server over the holiday.
Never install software from an unknown source.
She installed the shelf herself.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: The name and password used to enter an account.
practiceSentences: Keep your login private.
Has your login stopped working?
A shared login is nobody's responsibility.
She reset the login after the holiday.
The login screen appears before anything else.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: Sound, pictures, video and text used together.
practiceSentences: Her multimedia presentation used clips and charts.
What multimedia does the site include?
Multimedia holds attention better than text alone.
The multimedia room has speakers and a screen.
Too much multimedia distracts from the point.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: A message telling you that something has happened.
practiceSentences: A notification told her the file had saved.
How many notifications did you get today?
Turn off every notification while you work.
The notification arrived an hour too late.
One clear notification beats five vague ones.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: A newer version, or news of the latest position.
practiceSentences: The update fixes two known faults.
When is the next update due?
An update can break as well as mend.
She sent an update to the whole committee.
Install the update before the term starts.

words.group: Spelling: -tion, -ness, -ty and -ility
words.childMeaning: A guess about what will happen in the future.
practiceSentences: My prediction is that second-hand stalls will outnumber new-clothes stalls at next year's fair.
The analyst's prediction that natural fabrics would return to fashion proved accurate within two years.
What is your prediction for the clothing swap: fifty visitors or a queue around the block?
"My prediction," said Adam confidently, "is that repaired jeans will outsell new ones at the fair."
I wrote my prediction in my journal so I could later test my judgement against events.

words.group: Spelling: -tion, -ness, -ty and -ility
words.childMeaning: The heavy feeling you carry inside when something makes you unhappy.
practiceSentences: Talking about sadness can help another person feel understood.
Sadness filled the class when the holidays ended.
How do you chase sadness away on hard days?
Amara said, "Talking to Mum makes my sadness smaller."
I felt sadness when my best friend was ill.

words.group: Spelling: -tion, -ness, -ty and -ility
words.childMeaning: Being sure that something is true.
practiceSentences: We can say with certainty that the rains came late.
Is there any certainty in a long-range forecast?
Certainty is rarer in evidence than in argument.
She spoke with a certainty the figures did not support.
Certainty is a feeling; proof is a standard.

words.group: Spelling: -tion, -ness, -ty and -ility
words.childMeaning: The power or skill to do something.
practiceSentences: The school now has the capability to print its own magazine.
What capability does this project still need?
A capability unused is the same as one you do not have.
Their capability grew with every year of practice.
Capability is what you could do; capacity is how much.

words.group: Spelling: -tion, -ness, -ty and -ility
words.childMeaning: The state of being prepared and willing.
practiceSentences: Their readiness for the exhibition showed in every detail.
What readiness does a debate require?
Readiness is preparation plus willingness, and needs both.
She checked the team's readiness the evening before.
Readiness changes the y of ready to an i.

words.group: A word that names what must not happen
words.childMeaning: In case something unwanted should happen.
practiceSentences: Write it down lest you forget.
Should we check again, lest the figures be wrong?
She spoke quietly lest anyone overhear.
Keep a copy lest the original be lost.
Lest is followed by should, or by a plain verb.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: About ideas rather than things you can touch.
practiceSentences: Kindness is an abstract idea.
Which words in this list are abstract?
Abstract nouns name feelings and thoughts.
An abstract painting shows shapes, not objects.
Freedom is abstract; a gate is not.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The story of a person's life, written by that person.
practiceSentences: She wrote an autobiography about her childhood.
Whose autobiography did you read?
An autobiography uses the word 'I' throughout.
An autobiography is by you; a biography is not.
His autobiography begins in a small village.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A group of words containing a verb, part of a sentence.
practiceSentences: This sentence has two clauses.
Which clause is the main one?
A clause must contain a verb.
Join the two clauses with a comma.
The second clause explains the first.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The situation or background that helps you understand something.
practiceSentences: Read the whole page to find the context.
What context does the first chapter give?
Context helps you guess an unknown word.
Without context, the quotation is confusing.
The historical context explains her choice.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A short form of two words, written with an apostrophe.
practiceSentences: 'Don't' is a contraction of 'do not'.
Which contraction appears in this line?
A contraction needs an apostrophe.
Avoid a contraction in very formal writing.
'It's' is a contraction, not a possessive.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: Using words to mean more than they literally say.
practiceSentences: Calling the sea angry is figurative language.
Which line is figurative rather than literal?
Figurative writing makes a picture in your mind.
Poems often use figurative language.
A figurative phrase is not meant word for word.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A word that sounds like another but is spelled differently.
practiceSentences: 'Their' and 'there' are homophones.
Can you name a homophone for 'sea'?
A homophone can cause a spelling mistake.
'Two', 'to' and 'too' are homophones.
Check each homophone when you proofread.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A phrase whose meaning is not what the words say.
practiceSentences: 'Under the weather' is an idiom for unwell.
Which idiom did the author use?
An idiom can confuse a new reader.
Every language has its own idiom for luck.
Explain the idiom in your own words.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A conclusion you reach from clues rather than being told.
practiceSentences: Her inference came from the silent machines.
Which inference does the chapter support?
An inference must rest on evidence.
A strong inference joins a clue to what you know.
My first inference about the ending was wrong.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: Saying one thing is another to compare them.
practiceSentences: A metaphor says one thing is another.
What metaphor describes a thunderstorm?
The poet's metaphor called the class a beehive.
A metaphor uses no 'like' or 'as'.
Theo's metaphor described hands as gentle maps.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A story or description of events that tells what happened.
practiceSentences: The narrative kept me interested to the end.
What narrative does this picture suggest?
A narrative needs a beginning and an end.
She wrote her report as a narrative.
The narrative follows one family for a year.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The person who tells the story or describes the events in a book, film, or show.
practiceSentences: Amal practised her lines carefully before becoming the narrator for the show.
Who will be the narrator for our class film this term?
Sami, you would make a brilliant narrator!
A calm, clear narrator can make any story easy to follow.
The narrator's voice changes when each character speaks.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The act of getting somebody to agree with you.
practiceSentences: Her persuasion convinced the whole class.
What persuasion did the advert use?
Good persuasion uses reasons, not volume.
The letter was a piece of gentle persuasion.
Persuasion works best when you listen first.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: Words someone said or wrote, repeated by another person.
practiceSentences: Put the quotation inside speech marks.
Which quotation supports your point?
A quotation must be copied exactly.
She opened her essay with a quotation.
Give the page number after each quotation.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A mention of where information came from.
practiceSentences: Add a reference for every fact you use.
Which reference did you find most useful?
A reference lets a reader check your source.
The reference names the author and the year.
She made a reference to an earlier chapter.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The way the parts of a piece of writing are arranged.
practiceSentences: The structure of the essay is clear.
What structure does this poem follow?
A good structure guides the reader through.
Change the structure, not just the words.
The structure has an opening, middle and end.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A group of lines forming one section of a poem.
practiceSentences: The poem has four stanzas.
Which stanza repeats the opening line?
Each stanza has the same rhythm.
A blank line separates one stanza from the next.
Read the final stanza aloud.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The way a person sees or thinks about something.
practiceSentences: Write the story from Nora's viewpoint.
Whose viewpoint does the narrator take?
A different viewpoint can change the story.
Explain your viewpoint with clear reasons.
Two characters give opposite viewpoints.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: When several words close together begin with the same sound.
practiceSentences: 'Silver stars shine' uses alliteration.
Where is the alliteration in this line?
Alliteration makes a slogan easy to remember.
Poets use alliteration to link words.
Nora hunted for alliteration in shop signs.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A word that means the opposite of another word.
practiceSentences: 'Hot' is an antonym of 'cold'.
What is the antonym of 'ancient'?
An antonym helps you explain a meaning.
Write an antonym beside each word.
A synonym is close; an antonym is opposite.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A mark showing a missing letter or who owns something.
practiceSentences: An apostrophe shows the missing letter in 'don't'.
Where does the apostrophe go in this word?
Use an apostrophe to show that Amal owns it.
A missing apostrophe changes the meaning.
Check every apostrophe when you proofread.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A type of writing, music or film.
practiceSentences: Adventure is a popular genre.
Which genre do you read most often?
A mystery belongs to its own genre.
Each genre has its own patterns.
The library sorts books by genre.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A chance to do something worth doing.
practiceSentences: The trip was an opportunity she could not refuse.
What opportunity does this offer you?
An opportunity missed rarely returns unchanged.
He took the opportunity to ask his question.
Every problem carries an opportunity inside it.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A written agreement between two or more people or groups.
practiceSentences: Every player signed the team contract before the first match.
What happens if a builder breaks the contract with the town?
The astronauts signed a contract promising to follow safety rules.
"Read the whole contract before you sign anything," Father says.
Our class wrote a homework contract and everyone signed it.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The system by which a country makes and uses its money.
practiceSentences: The economy depends heavily on farming.
How has the economy changed since the drought?
A strong economy needs more than one industry.
The port is central to the local economy.
Economy also means using something carefully.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The making of goods, especially in factories.
practiceSentences: Fishing is the main industry along this coast.
Which industry employs the most people here?
Industry brought the railway to the valley.
The tourism industry grew after the road opened.
Industry also means steady, hard work.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The money a person earns from working or selling things.
practiceSentences: Jamal's income depended on how many fish he sold each day.
Does a market trader's income change with the seasons?
Their income barely covered the rent that month.
Teacher Yasmin explained how income and spending must balance.
A steady income is easier to plan around than a large one.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Hard work, or the people who do it.
practiceSentences: Harvest labour keeps the whole village busy for weeks.
Building the barn took months of hard labour.
Why does farm labour begin before the sun rises?
"Honest labour brings its own reward," said Grandfather.
I respect the labour that brings food to our table.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The money left after all the costs are paid.
practiceSentences: The stall made a small profit on market day.
What profit did the sale bring in?
Profit is income minus costs, and nothing else.
She put the profit back into the business.
A busy shop does not always make a profit.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A fixed amount paid regularly for a job.
practiceSentences: Her salary is paid on the last day of the month.
What salary does the post offer?
A salary is steady; a wage may vary by the hour.
He saved a tenth of his salary every month.
The salary was modest but the work suited her.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Money people pay to the government to fund public services.
practiceSentences: Tax pays for the roads and the schools.
How much tax is charged on this?
Everyone who earns above the threshold pays tax.
The council explained where the tax money went.
A tax on sugar was introduced last year.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The buying and selling of goods between people or countries.
practiceSentences: Trade between the two towns goes back centuries.
What goods does this trade involve?
Trade brought new words as well as new goods.
The port handles most of the country's trade.
She learned her trade from her grandmother.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Having paid work, or the work itself.
practiceSentences: The new factory brought employment to the village.
What employment is available here?
Employment rose after the road was finished.
She found employment within a month.
Employment gives more than money.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Things a person is entitled to by law or by fairness.
practiceSentences: Every child has rights, including the right to an education.
What rights does a tenant have?
Rights and duties belong together.
The class listed the rights they thought mattered most.
Rights are easiest to notice when they are missing.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Things a person is expected or required to do.
practiceSentences: Her duties include locking the gate each evening.
What duties come with the role?
Duties are the other half of rights.
He carried out his duties without complaint.
The list of duties was pinned to the door.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A tube that carries blood away from the heart.
practiceSentences: Every artery carries blood at high pressure.
Which artery is the largest in the body?
An artery has thicker walls than a vein.
You can feel an artery pulse in your wrist.
A blocked artery is a serious matter.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The movement of blood around the body.
practiceSentences: Exercise improves your circulation.
How long does one round of circulation take?
Cold hands can mean poor circulation.
The heart drives the whole circulation.
Circulation also means how widely a paper is read.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To do with breaking food down inside the body.
practiceSentences: The digestive system starts at the mouth.
Which digestive organ does most of the work?
Digestive juices break the food into pieces.
A digestive problem can follow a hurried meal.
She drew the digestive system in her notebook.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Keeping yourself and your surroundings clean in order to stay healthy.
practiceSentences: Does poor hygiene increase the risk of getting sick?
Sami's school teaches hygiene as part of health lessons.
What excellent hygiene the team showed after training in the mud!
Doctor Alina explained that hygiene is just as important as nutrition.
Good hygiene begins with washing your hands properly.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A sickness caused by germs that can spread.
practiceSentences: Nurses wash their hands so no infection passes between patients.
How does a doctor know if a small cut has an infection?
Washing your hands before meals helps stop infection spreading.
"Keep the plaster on so the infection cannot get worse," said the nurse.
Noah missed a whole week of school because of an ear infection.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A part of the body that does a particular job.
practiceSentences: The heart is the organ that pumps blood.
Which organ cleans the blood?
Each organ depends on the others.
The skin is the body's largest organ.
An organ is also a large musical instrument.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Poisonous, and harmful to living things.
practiceSentences: Some berries on that bush are toxic.
Is this cleaning fluid toxic?
Toxic waste must never reach the river.
The fumes proved toxic in a closed room.
A toxic plant may look perfectly harmless.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A medicine that trains the body to resist a disease.
practiceSentences: The vaccine protects against measles.
How long does the vaccine take to work?
A vaccine teaches the body before the illness arrives.
The clinic offered the vaccine to every family.
One vaccine can end an epidemic.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A long period with far too little rain.
practiceSentences: The drought lasted three growing seasons.
How do farmers prepare for a drought?
Drought empties the wells before it empties the rivers.
The drought forced families to move north.
Drought is measured in months, not days.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A great overflow of water onto normally dry land.
practiceSentences: The flood reached the second step of the school.
What causes a flood in this valley?
A flood can follow a drought within a week.
They moved the goats before the flood arrived.
Flood water is dangerous even when shallow.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A sudden violent shaking of the ground.
practiceSentences: The earthquake shook the whole valley for a minute.
How is the strength of an earthquake measured?
An earthquake gives almost no warning.
Buildings here are designed to survive an earthquake.
Two years after the earthquake, the town was rebuilt.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A mountain that can erupt with hot lava, ash, and gas.
practiceSentences: Scientists watch the volcano closely for smoke and small shakes.
Hot lava poured slowly down the side of the volcano.
How long has that volcano been quiet and still?
"Our model volcano will fizz and bubble," said Adam.
I built a clay volcano for the science fair.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Ready and happy to do something.
practiceSentences: Talia was willing to stay late to care for the injured animal.
Are the villagers willing to give up using snares?
Sami, thank you for being so willing to help!
The whole class seemed willing to volunteer at the reserve.
Local families now say they are willing to build better fences.
